comments.text:
If your curious why cooling a data centre in space is so hard well there’s 3 main ways of getting heat away from something.

I’ll start with conduction, it’s basically just the thermal transfer from one object to another that are touching, so when you touch something that’s conduction. 

The next is convection, this is thermal transfer using a fluid, so when you cook something in an oven, heat is transferred from the heating element to the air, then to the food, this is the most common way to cool things because you can easily increase the rate at which heat is exchanged by  by moving new fluid over the object to increase heat transfer (that’s why your PC, power stationers, data centres etc. use it), that’s why using a fan oven means you can use a lower temp to cook the same food, because it increases the rate at which the hot air transfers the heat to the food compared to the standing air of a no fan oven. 

Now if you notice those two methods require the objects to be touch another object or a form of fluid, none of which are in space, so that leave you with radiating the heat away, which is basically the atoms emitting electromagnetic waves as they move, and it SUCKS, for dispelling heat, like there is no sugar coating it, it’s so slow, not in terms of physical speed it move at the speed of light, but in terms of cooling something, and because of that you need a bunch of surface area to compensate for the slow rate. Also because anything that is good at emitting thermal radiation, is also good at absorbing it, you have to essentially hide the cooling area, so it’ll have to be behind the object you put in space, or continually stay on the other side of the earth from the sun, or the sun I’ll heat it up and change it from a cooling area, into one that makes the data centre hotter.

comments.text:
It's actually not super complicated to understand why you can't easily cool stuff in space, at least in broad strokes.

Tl;dr version is that in order to cool something, you need to put that excess heat somewhere. Your two options for carrying away heat are either 
A) radiating the energy as light, which necessarily generates even more waste heat, or 
B) transferring that heat into something else and getting rid of whatever that is.

The problem with option B) is that the vacuum of space is almost entirely empty - on earth, you can just blow air over a hot GPU and then that air is exhausted somewhere else. AC units on datacentres take the hot air from inside the building and transfer the heat outside the building to be vented off by and into the atmosphere (if ever you've stood behind a fridge or in front of an AC unit's exhaust and felt how warm it is, you've experienced this in action!), and fresh cool air is blown back over the GPUs restarting the cycle. You need a "reservoir" of cold stuff (e.g. an atmosphere, the ground, etc.) to actually put all the excess energy into, and the one thing outer space is famously lacking is any fucking stuff

In space, normal AC units like you see on earth simply aren't possible to build unless you have a constant delivery of fresh coolant to the satellite. Luckily all objects radiate some heat energy passively through what's known as Black Body Radiation; it's why the sun glows, it's why things glow red hot when you heat them up to hundreds of degrees. Thing is, at "normal" temperatures (i.e. the kinds of temperature the chips for a datacentre operate at, even in space), black body radiation is painfully weak. The only real option for running something like a server farm or GPU datacentre in space is to build an absolutely ENORMOUS heat transfer/radiator system, protected from solar heating, which you can run your coolant through and give it time to radiate away its heat. 

Suffice to say, the engineering challenges of building something like that are fucking insane to the point where it's hard to see how it could ever be commercially or logistically viable to put any kind of usefully sized datacentre infrastructure in space. Space is absolutely chock full of hazards like micrometeorites, especially in low earth orbit where we've been smashing satellites, old space stations, etc. into each other for the better part of almost 70 years now, and it's only getting worse from here, so good luck engineering a radiator system which is tough enough to resist micrometeorite impacts, but is also light enough to transport into space and also allows a reasonable heat transfer from the coolant into the casing to be radiated off.
